n: The Preacher describes another sad situation he has seen often among people.
A man may have riches, wealth, and honor — everything he wants — yet be unable to enjoy any of it, while a stranger ends up enjoying it instead. That is a kind of sickness.
Even a man with a hundred children and a very long life, if he never finds satisfaction and isn’t honored at death, is worse off than a stillborn child.

f.g: In Israel, lacking a proper burial was a great disgrace (Jeremiah 22:18-19).

n: The stillborn child comes into the world in futility, leaves in darkness, and its name is never known.

f.g: Arrives for nothing — its life passes as a breath.

n: It never saw the sun or knew anything, yet it has more rest than the restless, unsatisfied man.
Even living two thousand years would not help if a person never enjoyed any good. Everyone ends in the same grave.
People work hard to feed themselves, yet their hunger always returns. Earthly appetite can never be permanently filled.
What advantage does the wise person have over the fool, or the poor person who knows how to conduct himself well? From below, it’s hard to say.
Enjoying what is in front of you is better than endlessly craving what you don’t have. Restless desire is chasing the wind.

f.g: The roaming of the appetite; endless craving.

n: Everything that exists has already been named and defined, and humanity is known for what it is: mortal. No one can argue with God, who is stronger.

f.w: it is known that it is man
f.g: Possibly a play on Adam (“man”) from adamah (“ground”) — humans are made of earth.

f.w: contend with him that is mightier

n: The more words people use arguing with God or life, the more empty it becomes. Talking doesn’t make anyone better off.
Who knows what is truly good for a person in this brief, shadow-like life? And who can tell what will happen after he is gone? These questions prepare for the book’s conclusion.
